exp: Keats loved Fanny Brawne.

Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness

text: In which month and year did Keats write 'Ode to a Nightingale'?

The poetry of earth is never dead

My heart aches, and a drowsy numbness pains

A bright torch and a casement ope at night

Thou still unravish'd bride of quietness

Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness

Thou still unravish'd bride of quietness

My heart aches, and a drowsy numbness pains

When I Have Fears That I May Cease to Be

text: 'Ode to a Nightingale' consists of how many stanzas?

text: Each stanza of 'To Autumn' contains how many lines?

text: The rhyme scheme of 'Ode on Melancholy' is generally:

text: In 'Ode on Indolence', the three figures the speaker sees are:

text: In 'Ode on Indolence', the third figure, 'maiden most unmeek', is:

text: In 'Ode to a Nightingale', the bird is addressed as:

text: In 'Ode to a Nightingale', the speaker says he will fly to the bird 'on the viewless wings of':

text: The lines 'Charm'd magic casements, opening on the foam / Of perilous seas, in faery lands forlorn' occur in:

text: In 'Ode to a Nightingale', whose 'sad heart' is 'sick for home' amid 'the alien corn'?
exp: The bird's song reaches 'the sad heart of Ruth'.

text: 'Darkling I listen' appears in:

text: In 'Ode to a Nightingale', the speaker confesses he has been 'half in love with':
exp: He has been 'half in love with easeful Death'.

text: 'Heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard / Are sweeter' occurs in:

text: 'Bold Lover, never, never canst thou kiss' occurs in:
exp: The speaker addresses the frozen lover on the urn.

text: The apostrophe 'Cold Pastoral!' occurs in:

text: In the second stanza of 'To Autumn', Autumn is pictured 'Drows'd with the fume of':
exp: Autumn reposes 'Drows'd with the fume of poppies'.

text: The third stanza of 'To Autumn' begins:

Who hath not seen thee oft amid thy store?
Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness
Think not of them, thou hast thy music too

options: And gathering swallows twitter in the skies.

To let the warm Love in!

text: In 'Ode to Psyche', Psyche's lover, 'the winged boy', is:

exp: This line opens the evening imagery of the final stanza.

text: In the second stanza of 'To Autumn', Autumn is imagined as all of the following EXCEPT:
exp: Autumn appears as reaper, gleaner and watcher of the cider-press, not as a nightingale.

text: In 'To Autumn', 'Hedge-crickets sing; and now with treble soft / The red-breast':
exp: 'The red-breast whistles from a garden-croft'.

text: In 'Ode on Indolence', the speaker addresses the three figures as 'ye three':
exp: 'So, ye three Ghosts, adieu!'

text: The epigraph to 'Ode on Indolence' is:
options: 'They toil not, neither do they spin.'
ans: 'They toil not, neither do they spin.'
exp: The epigraph is from the Sermon on the Mount.

text: In 'Ode to Psyche', the poet sees two fair creatures 'couchèd side by side'; they are:
exp: The winged boy and Psyche lie side by side.

text: In 'Ode to Psyche', Psyche is the 'latest born' of:
exp: She is the last-born of the Olympian gods.

text: In 'Ode on Melancholy', the speaker warns against making 'Your mournful Psyche' out of:
exp: He rejects such deathly emblems of melancholy.

text: In 'Ode on Melancholy', the speaker tells us to 'glut thy sorrow on a':
exp: 'Then glut thy sorrow on a morning rose.'

text: 'Or on the wealth of globed peonies' occurs in:
exp: It is listed among the beautiful things to feed sorrow on.

text: 'Turning to poison while the bee-mouth sips' occurs in:
exp: Pleasure turns to poison in the third stanza.

text: In 'La Belle Dame sans Merci', the knight is described as 'Alone and':
exp: 'Alone and palely loitering' recurs at the close.

text: 'I see a lily on thy brow, / With anguish moist and fever-dew' occurs in:
exp: The speaker describes the knight's deathly pallor.

text: 'The squirrel's granary is full, / And the harvest's done' occurs in:
exp: The second stanza sets the wintry, post-harvest scene.

text: In 'La Belle Dame sans Merci', the lady fed the knight 'roots of relish sweet, / And honey wild, and':
exp: 'And honey wild, and manna-dew'.

text: 'The owl, for all his feathers, was a-cold' occurs in:
exp: The first stanza stresses the bitter cold.

text: In 'The Eve of St. Agnes', the heroine is:
exp: Madeline is the maiden who keeps St. Agnes' rites.

text: 'Into her dream he melted, as the rose / Blendeth its odour with the violet' refers, in 'The Eve of St. Agnes', to:
exp: Porphyro melts into Madeline's dream.

text: In 'The Eve of St. Agnes', when Madeline wakes she exclaims, 'How chang'd thou art! how':
exp: She finds the real Porphyro colder than her dream.

text: 'And she forgot the stars, the moon, and sun' occurs in:
options: Isabella; or, The Pot of Basil
ans: Isabella; or, The Pot of Basil
exp: Grief makes Isabella forget the world around her.

text: 'O Melancholy, turn thine eyes away!' occurs in:
options: Isabella; or, The Pot of Basil
ans: Isabella; or, The Pot of Basil
exp: The poet apostrophizes Melancholy in Isabella.

text: The refrain at the end of 'Isabella' is:
options: O cruelty, / To steal my Basil-pot away from me!
To let the warm Love in!
ans: O cruelty, / To steal my Basil-pot away from me!
exp: The poem ends with this lamenting refrain.

text: In 'Lamia', the serpent Lamia is described as a 'Gordian shape of dazzling hue, / Vermilion-spotted, golden, green, and':
exp: 'Vermilion-spotted, golden, green, and blue'.

text: In 'Lamia', the nymph whom Hermes seeks is made invisible by:
exp: Lamia had hidden the nymph from the satyrs.

text: In 'Lamia', Apollonius's fatal word to Lamia is simply:
exp: His cry 'A serpent!' destroys her.

text: 'An endless fountain of immortal drink, / Pouring unto us from the heaven's brink' occurs in:
exp: This image of beauty closes the famous opening of Endymion.

text: In 'Endymion', the shepherd Endymion lives on:
exp: Endymion is the shepherd-prince of Mount Latmos.

text: 'Saturn is fallen, am I too to fall?' is spoken in 'Hyperion' by:
exp: Hyperion, the still-powerful sun Titan, speaks these words.

text: In 'Hyperion', which Titan argues that they should accept defeat because the new gods are more beautiful?
exp: Oceanus counsels acceptance, finding Neptune more beautiful.

text: In 'The Fall of Hyperion', Moneta tells the poet-dreamer that 'None can usurp this height' except those to whom:
options: the miseries of the world / Are misery
ans: the miseries of the world / Are misery
exp: She says only those who feel the world's misery may ascend.

text: In 'Ode on a Grecian Urn', the 'happy melodist' is 'For ever piping songs for ever new' and is called:
exp: 'And, happy melodist, unwearied, / For ever piping songs for ever new'.

text: 'To Autumn' was composed in which year?
exp: It was written in September 1819, after a walk near Winchester.

text: Which of Keats's odes is a poem of pure, unanxious description of the season, often cited as an example of 'negative capability'?
exp: It dwells in the sensory world without anxious questioning.

text: In 'Ode to a Nightingale', the speaker imagines dying 'To cease upon the midnight with no pain' while the bird 'art pouring forth thy soul abroad / In such an':
exp: 'While thou art pouring forth thy soul abroad / In such an ecstasy!'

text: In 'Ode on a Grecian Urn', the figures on the urn are called 'marble men and maidens':
exp: 'with brede / Of marble men and maidens overwrought'.

text: In 'Ode on a Grecian Urn', the speaker says the little town's streets will be 'for evermore' silent because:
options: those who left it will never return
the urn does not show it
ans: those who left it will never return
exp: Its folk are frozen on the urn and can never return.

text: 'Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness' begins the poem with an example of:
options: trochaic inversion at the start of the line
ans: trochaic inversion at the start of the line
exp: A stressed syllable opens the line, an Augustan/trochaic inversion.

text: 'Ode to a Nightingale' was written at which house, where Keats also lived near Fanny Brawne?
exp: Keats wrote it at Wentworth Place, Hampstead.

text: In 'Ode to Psyche', the poet will become Psyche's priest and build her a fane 'In some untrodden region of my':
exp: He builds the temple 'In some untrodden region of my mind'.

text: In 'The Eve of St. Agnes', the lovers finally:
options: flee from the castle into the storm
ans: flee from the castle into the storm
exp: They escape into the wintry night.

text: 'Beauty is truth, truth beauty' is best described as:
exp: The phrase mirrors 'beauty' and 'truth' in reverse order.
